50.title: Nets on the right side (Luke 5:1–11)
50.hook: fishermen catch nothing all night, try once more, and the nets tear
50.howItsDone: Christians often call themselves disciples of Jesus, and many churches speak of discipleship as a lifelong apprenticeship through prayer, scripture, worship and service. The fish became one of the earliest Christian symbols.

segments.voice: Yesterday, temptation: bread, spectacle, power, and three refusals in the wilderness. Not by bread alone. And today is day fifty.

A lake at dawn, the Sea of Galilee. Some fishermen are pulling their boats up on the shore and washing their nets. They've been out all night, which is when you fished that lake, and they caught nothing. Not one fish. Anyone who has worked all night with nothing to show for it knows how they feel. They're tired, and they want to go home. Meanwhile a crowd is pressing in around a teacher on the beach, so many people he can hardly stand. He steps into one of the boats, the one that belongs to a fisherman named Simon, and asks him to push out a little.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING TO SHOW.` → `EMPTY NETS AT DAWN.` → `A TEACHER STEPS INTO SIMON'S BOAT.`

segments.voice: Jesus teaches the crowd from the boat. Then he turns to Simon, in the King James Bible: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught." Simon is the professional here; Jesus is a teacher from inland. Simon's answer is honest and tired: "Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net." Nevertheless. That one word is the hinge. He doesn't feel it. He does it anyway. The net fills so full it starts to tear. They wave to their partners, James and John, in the other boat, and both boats fill until they start to sink. Simon falls at his knees: "Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord." And Jesus says: "Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men." They pull the boats up on the shore, and, the story says, "they forsook all, and followed him." The best catch of their lives, left on the beach. Disciple, in the Greek of the Gospels, is mathetes: a learner, a student, an apprentice. The English comes from the Latin discipulus, from discere, to learn. A disciple isn't mainly a fan or a follower. It's someone who goes to school with a teacher, walking beside him, watching how he does things. The Gospels use the word for a wide circle of people, women and men, and from them Jesus chose twelve. Simon, the one who said nevertheless, will be called Peter. It all starts with one more try.
screen: `LAUNCH OUT INTO THE DEEP.` · `NEVERTHELESS AT THY WORD.` · `THE NETS BREAK.` · `A DISCIPLE IS A LEARNER.` · then, large: `THEY FORSOOK ALL, AND FOLLOWED HIM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you tried and gave up on, a conversation that went nowhere, a skill you dropped, a door you knocked on once, and hold it without blaming yourself. Ask whether there's one more try in you, just one, not forever, and picture letting down the net one more time. If you pray, you can say Simon's word: nevertheless.
Disciple. From the Latin for learner, and the Greek mathetes: a student who walks beside the teacher. Simon's first lesson was one more try.
Your line: put out into the deep. Fifty days on the path now, and still a learner.

51.title: The tax collector's party (Matthew 9:9–13)
51.hook: Jesus calls Matthew from his booth and eats with his shady friends
51.howItsDone: Many churches keep the feast of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, in September in the West and in November in the Orthodox calendar. Christians often point to this story when welcoming newcomers or sharing meals with people who are left out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, disciple: a learner, and fishermen who tried one more time and left full nets on the beach. Put out into the deep.

Every town has someone people avoid sitting next to. Maybe he cheated people. Maybe he works for someone everyone resents. Maybe it's just his reputation. In Capernaum, a fishing town on the lake, there's a booth by the road where goods passing through get taxed. The man in the booth is named Matthew. He collects money for the rulers who answer to Rome, and people assume tax collectors take extra for themselves. The Gospel doesn't say whether he did. Jesus walks past, stops, and looks right at him.
screen: `THE ONE NOBODY SITS NEXT TO.` → `A BOOTH BY THE ROAD.` → `JESUS STOPS.`

segments.voice: Two words, in the King James Bible: "Follow me. And he arose, and followed him." No speech. No conditions. Matthew gets up. Then comes the party. Matthew opens his house for a meal, and many publicans and sinners come and sit down with Jesus and his disciples. Publican is the old word for tax collector. Sinners here means people known for breaking the law, the ones good families kept at a distance. Some Pharisees see it. They were serious, devout teachers who cared deeply about keeping God's law in everyday life, including who you ate with, because sharing a table meant sharing a life. So they ask the disciples: "Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?" It's a real question, and Jesus gives a real answer: "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick." A doctor who avoids sick people isn't much of a doctor. Then he quotes the prophet Hosea: "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice." Go and learn what that means, he says. And: "for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Notice where the calling happens. Not in the temple. At a tax booth, and then at a dinner table. In Mark and Luke the man at the booth is called Levi, and Christian tradition has long said this Matthew is the one whose name is on the first Gospel, though scholars still discuss who wrote it. Either way, the Gospel that bears his name tells his calling in one sentence. He got up.

segments.voice: Think about your table, whatever that means for you, your lunch spot, your group chat, the people you text back first, and then of someone who's never there: a coworker who eats alone, a neighbor you've never really met, a relative people roll their eyes at. Picture sharing one ordinary meal with them, and what you might talk about. If you pray, you can name that person in your prayer.
Publican. The old King James word for tax collector, what the crowd called Matthew before Jesus looked at him and said, follow me.
Your line: he came for the sick. Tomorrow, another party, and this time the wine runs out.

52.title: Water into wine (John 2:1–11)
52.hook: a wedding runs dry; Mary tells the servants to do whatever he says
52.howItsDone: Many churches read the wedding at Cana at weddings and in the weeks after Epiphany, and Catholics pray it as the second luminous mystery of the rosary. Many Christians see in it a blessing on marriage and on ordinary celebrations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a publican's table, full of people others kept away from. He came for the sick.

A cake collapses. A band doesn't show. Weddings go wrong. Here's one in Cana, a village in Galilee. Jesus is there with his first disciples, and his mother too. In the middle of the feast, the wine runs out. Historians of the period say that would have embarrassed the hosts badly, since a wedding feast put a family's hospitality on display. John doesn't explain any of that. He says only that the wine ran short, and that the mother of Jesus spoke up.
screen: `A WEDDING GOING WRONG.` → `CANA, IN GALILEE.` → `THE WINE RUNS OUT.`

segments.voice: She goes to her son with four words: "They have no wine." Just the need, laid in front of him. His answer sounds sharp to our ears: "Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come." But woman wasn't rude in his language; it was a respectful way to address someone, and he'll call her the same thing from the cross. Then Mary does something unexpected. She doesn't argue. She tells the servants: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." Those are her last recorded words in John's Gospel. And John never gives her name; she's always the mother of Jesus. Six stone water jars stand there, the kind used for washing by the rules of purity, each holding, the King James says, two or three firkins. That's a lot of water. Fill them, he says, and they fill them to the brim. Now draw some out and take it to the head of the feast. It's wine. The man in charge, not knowing where it came from, calls the bridegroom over, puzzled: everyone serves the good wine first, and the cheap stuff after people have had plenty, but "thou hast kept the good wine until now." The King James calls it the beginning of miracles, but John's Greek word is semeion, a sign: something that points past itself. This is the first. Christians read Mary's part in different ways. Catholics and Orthodox Christians often see her here bringing people's needs to her son. Many Protestants dwell on how she points away from herself: do whatever he tells you.
screen: `THEY HAVE NO WINE.` · `WHATSOEVER HE SAITH UNTO YOU, DO IT.` · `SIX STONE JARS, FILLED TO THE BRIM.` · `THE FIRST OF HIS SIGNS.` · then, large: `THOU HAST KEPT THE GOOD WINE UNTIL NOW.`

segments.voice: Think of a celebration coming up or going on now, a birthday, a new baby, a friend's small win, a wedding, a holiday meal, and look at it the way Mary looked at the wedding: where is the wine running low, who's doing all the work, who's quietly worried it won't be enough? Notice one place that needs a hand. If you pray, you can bring it to God in four words: they have no wine.
Semeion. John's Greek word for sign, something that points past itself, which is what he calls this first wonder at a wedding in Cana.
Your line: do whatever he tells you. Tomorrow, a woman at a well, at noon. Day fifty-two counts.

53.title: The woman at the well (John 4:1–30)
53.hook: at noon, alone, a Samaritan woman has a long conversation with Jesus across an old divide
53.howItsDone: Many churches read the woman at the well during Lent, and Orthodox Christians keep a Sunday of the Samaritan Woman in the Easter season, honoring her as Saint Photini. Christians often read the story when speaking of baptism and of welcoming people across divides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, water into wine: John's first semeion, a sign that points past itself, and a mother saying do whatever he tells you.

A stranger on a train. A seatmate at a wedding. Sometimes the real talk is with someone nobody planned to meet. This one happens at a well in Samaria, about the sixth hour, John says: noon, the heat at its worst. Jesus, tired from walking, sits on the edge of the well while his disciples go into town for food. A woman comes out with a jar to draw water. Alone. And he speaks to her.
screen: `A CONVERSATION YOU DIDN'T EXPECT.` → `NOON, AT THE WELL.` → `A WOMAN COMES ALONE.`

segments.voice: He says, in the King James Bible: "Give me to drink." She's startled: "How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans." Jews and Samaritans shared ancestors and the books of Moses, but had long been divided over where to worship God: Jerusalem, or Mount Gerizim, right above this well. A Jewish teacher didn't usually ask a Samaritan woman for a drink. He answers: "If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water." Here's the wordplay. Living water, in Greek and in everyday speech then, meant running water, fresh from a spring, not still water in a cistern. She hears the plain meaning: you don't even have a bucket. He means water that becomes "a well of water springing up into everlasting life." Then he tells her about her own life: five husbands, and now a man who isn't her husband. Some preachers have assumed she was a scandal, and that's why she came at noon. The text never says why. A woman then could be widowed, or sent away by a husband; John doesn't say what happened. What John does record is about twenty verses of question and answer, and it's with her. She goes back to town, leaving her jar behind: "Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" Orthodox Christians remember her as Photini, the enlightened one.
screen: `GIVE ME TO DRINK.` · `A JEW ASKS A SAMARITAN.` · `LIVING WATER MEANS RUNNING WATER.` · `SHE LEAVES HER JAR.` · then, large: `A WELL OF WATER SPRINGING UP.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you mostly talk to in passing, a parent, a coworker, a neighbor, someone who serves you coffee, and picture sitting down with them, no clock, no phone. What might you ask that you never have, and what might they tell you? If you pray, you can ask for patience to listen.
Samaritan. The woman Jesus meets at the well, from a people long divided from the Jews, whom he still asks, in the heat of noon, for a drink.
Your line: living water. Tomorrow, a hillside, a hungry crowd and a boy's lunch. Day fifty-three, done.

54.title: A boy's lunch (John 6:1–14)
54.hook: five loaves and two fish from a child, and five thousand eat with baskets left over
54.howItsDone: Many churches read the feeding of the five thousand alongside teaching about communion and about sharing with people in need. Some church meals and food programs point to this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Samaritan woman at a well, and a long talk at noon about living water.

Not enough money for the month. Not enough time. Not enough patience for the kids tonight. Some sums never add up. Here's one on a grassy hillside by the Sea of Galilee. A huge crowd has followed Jesus there, because they've seen him heal the sick. Thousands of them, and nothing to eat. Jesus turns to one of his disciples, Philip, and asks a question John says was a test: where are we going to buy bread for all these people?
screen: `OBVIOUSLY NOT ENOUGH.` → `A HUNGRY CROWD ON A HILLSIDE.` → `WHERE SHALL WE BUY BREAD?`

segments.voice: Philip does the math, in the King James Bible: "Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little." A penny there is a denarius, a laborer's day's wage in one of Jesus's parables: two hundred days' wages, and still not a bite each. Then Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, comes back with something almost funny: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" Only John mentions the boy. Barley, some readers point out, was the cheaper grain. This is a kid's packed lunch, and somebody has to hand it over. Jesus has the people sit on the grass, about five thousand men, John says. He takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. Then a quieter line: "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost." They fill twelve baskets with leftovers. Twelve, from five loaves. Matthew, Mark and Luke tell this feeding too; it's in all four Gospels. Christians read it as a wonder, and some also hear in it the table of communion: he takes bread, gives thanks, and gives it. Later in the chapter he calls himself the bread of life. But start with the boy. Nobody asks him to fix the problem. He offers what he has, small as it is, and it turns out to be enough, with baskets to spare.
screen: `TWO HUNDRED DAYS' WAGES, NOT ENOUGH.` · `FIVE BARLEY LOAVES, TWO FISH.` · `HE GIVES THANKS AND GIVES.` · `TWELVE BASKETS LEFT OVER.` · then, large: `THAT NOTHING BE LOST.`

segments.voice: Think of a need you know about right now, a struggling friend, a cause you care about, a tired colleague, a lonely family member. Instead of everything it would take, look at what you actually have, ten minutes, a skill, a spare meal, a kind word, your five loaves and two fish, and picture handing it over. If you pray, you can give thanks for it first, the way he did.
Fragments. The broken pieces gathered up after the crowd ate their fill, twelve baskets of them, so that nothing from five loaves and two fish would be lost.
Your line: it was enough. Five loaves, two fish, twelve baskets left over. See you tomorrow.

55.title: The storm (Luke 8:22–25)
55.hook: the boat is swamping, Jesus is asleep, and the disciples shout him awake
55.howItsDone: Many Christians turn to this story in times of fear and illness, and it's often read at services for people at sea. The image of the church as a ship shows up in church architecture, in hymns, and in the name nave for the main hall.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy's lunch: five loaves, two fish, and twelve baskets of fragments. It was enough.

Three in the morning, when a worry gets loud: the bill, the diagnosis, the text you shouldn't have sent. Everything is going under, and everyone else seems asleep. Now a fishing boat on the Sea of Galilee. Jesus says, let's go over to the other side, and they push off. The lake sits low among hills, and storms can drop onto it fast. As they sail, Luke says, Jesus falls asleep. Then the wind comes down, the waves come over the side, and the boat fills with water. These are fishermen who know this lake, and they're terrified.
screen: `3AM, AND EVERYTHING'S GOING UNDER.` → `HE FALLS ASLEEP.` → `THE BOAT FILLS WITH WATER.`

segments.voice: They wake him with a shout, in the King James Bible: "Master, master, we perish." Mark's telling is rawer: "Master, carest thou not that we perish?" Don't you care? It's one of the most honest prayers in the Bible, shouted at a sleeping man in a sinking boat, and the text doesn't scold them for it. Then Luke says: "he arose, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water: and they ceased, and there was a calm." Mark gives his words to the sea: "Peace, be still." He talks to the storm the way you'd calm a frightened animal. Then comes a silence so big it frightens them in a new way; Mark says they feared exceedingly. He asks: "Where is your faith?" And they whisper to each other: "What manner of man is this! for he commandeth even the winds and water, and they obey him." In the Hebrew scriptures, the one who stills the sea is God. One psalm says of sailors in a storm: "He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still." That's the question the story leaves in the boat: who is this? Christians have long seen the church as a boat on rough water, and the main hall of many church buildings is still called the nave, from the Latin for ship. One more thing: he was in the boat the whole time. Asleep, but there. The story doesn't promise there'll be no storms. It puts him in the same wet boat as everyone else.
screen: `MASTER, CAREST THOU NOT?` · `HE REBUKED THE WIND.` · `WHAT MANNER OF MAN IS THIS?` · `THE NAVE: THE CHURCH AS A BOAT.` · then, large: `PEACE, BE STILL.`

segments.voice: Feel your feet on the floor and name the storm you're in, the specific one that keeps you up, quietly out loud in one sentence, plain, the way the disciples said it. Then take three slow breaths, letting your shoulders drop on each out-breath. If you pray, you can shout it honestly, as they did, or say Peace, be still; if you don't, let the breath be the calm.
The storm. A swamping boat, a sleeping teacher, a shout of don't you care, and a calm that frightened them all over again.
Your line: peace, be still. Three words to a storm, and then a calm. That's day fifty-five.

56.title: Peter walks on water (Matthew 14:22–33)
56.hook: Peter steps out, looks at the wind, sinks, and is caught by the hand
56.tomorrow: Who do you say I am?
56.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Peter's words, Lord, save me, in moments of fear, and the story is often preached on trust and doubt. Icons and paintings of the scene show Christ's hand reaching for Peter as he sinks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the storm: a sleeping teacher, an honest shout, and peace, be still. Today closes week eight and the road through Galilee.

The first day of a new job. Asking someone out. Standing up to speak. There's a moment where you step out or don't. Back to the lake, the same night as the boy's lunch. Jesus sends the disciples ahead in the boat and goes up a mountain alone to pray. Out on the water the wind is against them, and the waves toss the boat. Then, Matthew says, in the fourth watch of the night, the last stretch before dawn, they see him coming toward them, walking on the sea. They scream. They think it's a ghost.
screen: `THE MOMENT BEFORE YOU STEP OUT.` → `THE FOURTH WATCH OF THE NIGHT.` → `A FIGURE WALKING ON THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Straightaway he speaks, in the King James Bible: "Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid." And Peter, of course it's Peter, answers: "Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water." One word comes back: come. Peter climbs over the side, and actually walks. Then: "But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me." That's the whole shape of it. He steps out, looks at the wind instead of the one he's walking toward, and sinks. A three-word prayer, no time for more. Then: "And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?" Immediately. The hand comes first, the question after. Little faith, in Matthew's Greek, is one word, oligopistos, almost a nickname; Matthew's Jesus uses it for his disciples more than once. Little faith, not no faith: enough to step out, not quite enough to keep looking up. When they climb back in, the wind stops, and the people in the boat worship him and say, of a truth thou art the Son of God. So end two weeks on the road through Galilee: stargazers, a family fleeing, a boy asking questions, a wild man, a river, a desert, full nets, a party, a wedding, a well, a lunch, a storm. And now a man sinking, and a hand.
